1
INTEREST OF AMICI STATES
States bear primary responsibility for the criminal
justice system in the United States. They have a deep
interest in the stability and predictability of that system.
The Court in Williams v. Florida , 399 U.S. 78 (1970),
undertook the appropriate textual and historical analysis,
then adopted a clear, supportable rule. Amici States
write to emphasize that if the interests of stare decisis
are overcome based on mere disagreement with the
supportable but arguable result in Williams, the Court
should be willing to revisit other criminal procedure rules
from the 1960s and 1970s that have far less—indeed,
no—support in text or history, and that never should have
been incorporated against the States.
BACKGROUND
Fifty-six years ago, this Court undertook a detailed
historical and textual analysis of the Sixth Amendment,
then “conclude[d] that . . . Sixth Amendment rights, as
applied to the States through the Fourteenth Amendment,
were not violated by Florida’s decision to provide a sixman rather than a 12-man jury.” Williams, 399 U.S. at
103. Then, as now, Florida law generally provided for
six-person juries in criminal cases: “Twelve persons shall
constitute a jury to try all capital cases, and six persons
shall constitute a jury to try all other criminal cases.”
Fla. Stat. § 913.10.
Consistent with this Court’s holding in Williams ,
Petitioner Hamed Kian was convicted by a six-person
jury of practicing chiropractic medicine with a suspended
license, a crime punishable by up to five years in prison for

2
each of the five counts on which he was convicted. See Fla.
Stat. §§ 460.411(1)(b), 775.082(3)(e). Petitioner appealed his
convictions, arguing, inter alia, that the use of a six-person
jury violated his rights under the Sixth and Fourteenth
Amendments. The Florida District Court of Appeal
affirmed his convictions without a written opinion, 421
So.3d 439 (Fla. Dist. Ct. App. 2025), with the procedural
result that the Florida Supreme Court lacked jurisdiction
to review the decision.
This Court granted certiorari. As framed by
Petitioner, the question presented is whether he “was
deprived of his right, under the Sixth and Fourteenth
Amendments, to a trial by a 12-person jury.”
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
A 12-person jury was the prevailing norm at the time
of American Independence, but English law was rife
with exceptions. In drafting the Constitution and the Bill
of Rights, Congress was focused on the right to a jury
trial, yet it removed a provision requiring “accustomed
requisites” from a draft of the Sixth Amendment. That
may very well cut both ways. See Ramos v. Louisiana ,
590 U.S. 83, 97-98 (2020).  But Williams considered that
specific issue. 399 U.S. at 94-96. The historical record
was inconclusive. Id. Then, after analyzing the purpose
of the jury trial, Williams correctly concluded that the
12-person element wasn’t an indispensable feature.  Id.
at 97.
This Court undertook the appropriate historical
and textual analysis in Williams , then held the Sixth
Amendment did not incorporate the 12-person requirement.
Petitioner disagrees with that long-established result.

3
But disagreement with an arguable point is no reason to
depart from stare decisis .
To the extent the Court does overrule Williams, the
same arguments far-more-clearly call for this Court to
revisit much of the criminal procedure revolution of the
1960s and 1970s. Petitioner’s amici acknowledge as much,
with Professor Amar identifying Miranda v. Arizona, 384
U.S. 436 (1966), as a prime candidate for reconsideration.
This Court’s micromanagement of jury proceedings and
the byzantine capital punishment standards set forth in
Gregg v. Georgia, 428 U.S. 153 (1976), and its progeny are
similarly ripe for reconsideration, both on the merits and
as matter of incorporation.
ARGUMENT
I.  That Williams  drew a clear line in the face of
evidence supporting both sides is no reason to
revisit it.
This case ultimately asks whether the word “jury”
in the Sixth Amendment necessarily requires a body of
twelve citizens, and—if so—whether that requirement
is incorporated against the States via the Fourteenth
Amendment.
1. Start with history. Petitioner compiles an
impressive collection of historical claims, although none
are new. Pet. Br. 5-12. He correctly suggests that decisions
were made by bodies of citizens far into the past. But by
relying almost exclusively on tertiary sources, he muddles
the question by unknowingly pointing to the inquisitorial
forerunner of the grand jury as set forth in the Assize of

4
Clarendon, which directed inquests “by twelve of the most
legal men of the hundred, and by four of the most legal men
of each vill.” George Burton Adams & H. Morse Stephens
eds., Select Documents of English Constitutional History
14-15 (1901). The resulting trial was by ordeal of water. In
1176, the Assize of Northampton adopted a preference for
knights to lead the inquest. Id. 20-21. And it made clear
that surviving the ordeal merely reduced the punishment
to banishment from the kingdom rather than amputation
of a hand and foot before banishment, i.e., the inquest—
the forerunner of the grand jury—effectively determined
guilt. Id.
 In 1215, the Fourth Lateran Council prohibited clergy
from participating in trial by ordeal. That led Henry III
to ban such trials in toto. Thus began the common use of
petit juries. See Thomas A. Green, Verdict According to
Conscience: Perspectives on the English Criminal Jury
Trial 1200-1800 3 (1985). As English law evolved over the
following centuries, a twelve-man petit jury became a
common mode of trying serious criminal matters. 1
By the time of Henry VII, the press of criminal
cases and the attendant cost had become unmanageable.
Parliament responded by authorizing justices to
hear, determine, and punish non-felony offenses upon
information, i.e., without indictment, and without a trial
1. Kian ties the origin of the petit jury to Magna Carta, Pet.
Br. 6, a link that Felix Frankfurter characterized as “one of the
most revered of legal fables” and “an obstinate example of the
inevitable habit of reading later ideas into earlier institutions.”
Felix Frankfurter & Thomas G. Corcoran, Petty Offenses and
the Constitutional Guaranty of Trial by Jury , 39 hArv. L. rev.
917, 924-925 (1926).

5
by jury. 11 Hen. VII c.3 (reprinted in 2 The Statutes of
the Realm 570 (1816, reprinted 1963)). That authority was
nominally discretionary, but Sir Edward Coke’s “gloss
. . . attributes to this statute ‘most grievous and heavy
oppressions. . . .’” Frankfurter & Corcoran, supra  at
924 (quoting 4 Edward Coke, Institutes of the Laws of
England 41 (1817)). The statute was accordingly repealed
after Henry VII’s death. Still, legislation continued
to make “piecemeal inroads upon trial by jury,” with
“Parliament gradually adopt[ing] the practice of providing
that convictions . . . should be by one or more justices,”
and doing so for offenses of ever-greater moment. Id. at
925-926. Indeed, “the practice . . . became characteristic
of the jurisprudence of the country.” Id.
In 1671, for example, a statute made the night-time
burning of ricks, houses, and barns a felony punishable by
death or transportation, and subject to inquiry by three
justices instead of a jury. 22 & 23 Car. II c.7 (reprinted in
5 The Statutes of the Realm  709 (1819, reprinted 1963)).
Similarly, a 1717 statute made the unlawful exporting
of wool—hardly the stuff of malum in se —summarily
punishable by transportation if the defendant could not
post bail, with return to Great Britain punishable by
death. 4 Geo. 1 c.11. In short, the use of non-jury trials
was not-uncommon, even where serious penalties were on
the table. The practice, however, was erratic. “Down to
the separation of the colonies from the mother country,”
“there was no unifying consideration as to the type of
criminal offense subjected to summary trial.” Corcoran
& Frankfurter, supra, at 927.
2. In America, the colonies broke from England’s
centuries of legal evolution by adopting written constitutions.

6
At the time of Independence, the constitutions of at least
ten of those constitutions included some reference to the
right to trial by jury. See Ramos , 590 U.S. at 90. The
Pennsylvania Constitution of 1776, for example, provided
“that in all prosecutions for criminal offences, a man hath
a right to . . . a speedy public trial, by an impartial jury
of the country, without the unanimous consent of which
jury he cannot be found guilty,” and that “[t]rials shall be
by jury as heretofore . . . ” Similarly, the Massachusetts
Constitution of 1780 provided that “the legislature shall
not make any law, that shall subject any person to a capital
or infamous punishment . . . without trial by jury.” The
Virginia Declaration of Rights, however, was more specific.
It provided “[t]hat in all capital or criminal prosecutions a
man has a right . . . to a speedy trial by an impartial jury
of twelve men of his vicinage, without whose unanimous
consent he cannot be found guilty. . . .”
The practice of governing via a written constitution
continued when the States formed a national government.
Given their hostility to the deprivations of the right to a
jury trial under the Stamp Act of 1765, 5 Geo. 3 c.12, the
Townshend Revenue Act of 1766, 7 Geo. 3 c.46, and the
more-vigorously enforced Navigation Acts, the States
enshrined that right in the Constitution:
The Trial of all Crimes, except in Cases of
Impeachment, shall be by Jury; and such
Trial shall be held in the State where the said
Crimes shall have been committed; but when
not committed within any State, the Trial shall
be at such Place or Places as the Congress may
by Law have directed.
U.S. Const. art. III, § 2, cl. 3.

7
Still, the ratifying conventions of a number of
the States “expressed a desire, in order to prevent
misconstruction or abuse of [the Constitution’s] powers,
that further declaratory and restrictive clauses should be
added. . . .” Joint Resolution of Sept. 25, 1789. Congress
apparently concluded that Article III’s reference to “trial
. . . by jury” was among the provisions that were ambiguous
and in need of clarification. It accordingly proposed what
became the Fifth, Sixth, and Seventh amendments:
No person shall be held to answer for a capital,
or otherwise infamous crime, unless on a
presentment or indictment of a Grand Jury
. . . nor shall any person be subject for the same
offence to be twice put in jeopardy of life or
limb; nor shall be compelled in any criminal
case to be a witness against himself, nor be
deprived of life, liberty, or property, without
due process of law. . . .
In all criminal prosecutions, the accused shall
enjoy the right to a speedy and public trial,
by an impartial jury of the State and district
wherein the crime shall have been committed,
which district shall have been previously
ascertained by law, and to be informed of
the nature and cause of the accusation; to be
confronted with the witnesses against him;
to have compulsory process for obtaining
witnesses in his favor, and to have the
Assistance of Counsel for his defence.
In Suits at common law, where the value in
controversy shall exceed twenty dollars, the

8
right of trial by jury shall be preserved, and
no fact tried by a jury, shall be otherwise reexamined in any Court of the United States,
than according to the rules of the common law.
Joint Resolution of Sept. 25, 1789.
3. As this Court undertook the criminal procedure
revolution under Chief Justices Warren and Burger, it
was pressed to define the scope of those rights and how
they applied to the States. The mere reference to a “jury”
or “trial by jury” likely wasn’t unambiguous given that
Congress elaborated on the Article III jury right via
three separate, highly detailed amendments. Cf. Hurtado
v. California , 110 U.S. 516, 534-535 (1884) (applying the
superfluity canon to the Fifth Amendment). Justice Story
recognized another interpretive problem early in the
Nation’s history: even taking common law practices as the
baseline, the common law vis-à-vis juries “probably differs
in all” of the States, such that the Constitution must look
to “the common law of England” as it existed at the time
of independence. United States v. Wonson, 28 F . Cas. 745,
750 (Cir. Ct. Mass. 1812). But that merely deepens the
confusion given that English historical practices were rife
with exceptions, supra, notwithstanding the superlatives
and absolutes recounted by Coke and Blackstone. Still, the
criminal justice system required answers. So this Court
drew readily-workable lines.
4. Petitioner asks this Court to reconsider one such
line: this Court’s conclusion in Williams “that the 12-man
panel is not a necessary ingredient of ‘trial by jury,’ and

9
that respondent’s refusal to impanel more than the six
members provided for by Florida law did not violate [a
defendant’s] Sixth Amendment rights.” 399 U.S. at 86.
In Williams, this Court explained that English and
American history “revealed a long tradition attaching
great importance to the concept of relying on a body of
one’s peers to determine guilt or innocence as a safeguard
against arbitrary law enforcement.” Id. at 87. “That
same history, however, affords little insight into the
considerations that gradually led the size of that body to
be generally fixed at 12.” Id.
Turning to the Constitution itself, the Court explained
that “[t]he relevant constitutional history [also] casts
considerable doubt on the easy assumption . . . that if a
given feature existed in a jury at common law in 1789,
then it was necessarily preserved in the Constitution.”
Id. at 92. “Indeed, pending and after the adoption of
the Constitution, fears were expressed that Article III’s
provision failed to preserve the common-law right to be
tried by a ‘jury of the vicinage.’ Id. at 93. “That concern,
as well as the concern to preserve the right to jury in civil
as well as criminal cases, furnished part of the impetus
for introducing amendments to the Constitution that
ultimately resulted in the jury trial provisions of the Sixth
and Seventh Amendments.” Id. at 93-94. Not surprisingly,
there was great focus on the “vicinage” requirement. See
id. at 93-98. Yet there was no evidence that the number
of jurors was considered significant, and a requirement
for preserving the “accustomed requisites” was rejected.
The Court thus reached three conclusions. “First, even
though the vicinage requirement was as much a feature

10
of the common-law jury as was the 12-man requirement,
the mere reference to ‘trial by jury’ in Article III was not
interpreted to include that feature.” Id. at 96. “Indeed, as
the subsequent debates over the Amendments indicate,
disagreement arose over whether the feature should be
included at all in its common-law sense, resulting in the
compromise described above” regarding vicinage. Id.
“Second, provisions that would have explicitly tied the
‘jury’ concept to the ‘accustomed requisites’ of the time
were eliminated.” Id. “Such action is concededly open to
the explanation that the ‘accustomed requisites’ were
thought to be already included in the concept of a ‘jury.’”
Id. “But that explanation is no more plausible than the
contrary one: that the deletion had some substantive
effect.” Id. “Indeed, given the clear expectation that a
substantive change would be effected by the inclusion
or deletion of an explicit ‘vicinage’ requirement, the
latter explanation is, if anything, the more plausible.”
Id. “Finally, contemporary legislative and constitutional
provisions indicate that where Congress wanted to leave
no doubt that it was incorporating existing common-law
features of the jury system, it knew how to use express
language to that effect.” Id.2
This Court reaffirmed that conclusion three years
later in Colgrove v. Battin , 413 U.S. 149 (1973). The
Court explained that “Constitutional history does not
reveal a single instance where concern was expressed
for preservation of the traditional number 12.” Id. at 156
n.10. Thus, notwithstanding the Seventh Amendment’s
2. The difference between the jury provision in the wellknown Virginia Declaration of Rights, supra , and the Sixth
Amendment reinforces this Court’s conclusion.

11
“preserv[ing] the right of trial by jury as at common law,”
the Court concluded the Framers were concerned with the
“right of trial by jury . . . rather than the various incidents
of trial by jury” such as a panel of 12 jurors. Id. at 155-156.
The Constitution’s silence regarding the number
of jurors speaks volumes—there is no magic number.
Moreover, there is no basis for incorporating such an
imaginary number to the states as a fundamental right
under the Due Process Clause.
5. The question having been decided, “stare decisis
is the preferred course,” and this Court “will not overturn
a past decision unless there are strong grounds for doing
so.” Janus v. AFSCME, 585 U.S. 878, 916-917 (2018). The
Court’s cases “identify factors that should be taken into
account in deciding whether to overrule a past decision.”
Id. at 917. Those factors include “the nature of the error,”
Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Org., 597 U.S. 215, 268
(2022), “the quality of [the prior precedent’s] reasoning,
the workability of the rule it established, its consistency
with other related decisions, developments since the
decision was handed down, and reliance on the decision,”
Janus, 585 U.S. at 917.
Despite incanting some of those factors, Petitioner’s
analysis boils down to mere disagreement with the line this
Court drew in Williams. His brief brings nothing new to
the table. Rather, Petitioner merely catalogues resources
that were equally available to this Court in Williams
and Colgrove, and pleads for the opposite result. Indeed,
Petitioner makes no effort to grapple with the textual and
historical analysis in Williams. His unhappiness with the
line the Court drew doesn’t demonstrate error; it doesn’t

12
demonstrate poor reasoning; it doesn’t undercut the
workability of the Court’s line; and it doesn’t undercut the
States’ reliance on that line. Perhaps the current Court
would reach a different result if writing on a clean slate.
See Ramos , 590 U.S. at 96-98. But that’s no ground for
overruling precedent.
II.  If the Court intends to reopen Williams, it should
be willing to reopen the far-less-reasoned cases of
the criminal procedure revolution.
To be clear: Petitioner asks the Court to re-open a
clear, bright-line rule that resolved a question on solid
historical grounds while acknowledging that the history
was inconclusive. He then asks the Court incorporate a
new, opposite rule against the States. Of course, when a
precedent is overruled, it tends not to fall alone. See Dobbs,
597 U.S. at 265. Acknowledging as much, Petitioner’s
amici try to ringfence the carnage and buttress rules
they support. See Br. of Akhil Reed Amar. But if reversals
based on changed views are the course the Court intends
to set, the course should be steered true, without deviation
for the faint-hearted. Textualism, federalism, and fairness
demand the Court also re-open much of the so-called
criminal procedure revolution.
1. Professor Amar identifies the most obvious
candidate: Miranda v. Arizona , 384 U.S. 436 (1966). In
that case—wholly unmoored from the Constitution’s text
and the Nation’s historical practice—the Court “concluded
that without proper safeguards the process of in-custody
interrogation of persons suspected or accused of crime
contains inherently compelling pressures which work to
undermine the individual’s will to resist and to compel him

13
to speak where he would not otherwise do so freely.” Id. at
467. Acting prophylactically “to combat these pressures
and to permit a full opportunity to exercise the privilege
against self-incrimination,” the Court simply declared
ex cathedra  that “the accused must be adequately and
effectively apprised of his rights and the exercise of those
rights must be fully honored.” Id. That pronouncement
became the basis for ever increasing contortions to defend
a “constitutional rule” that wasn’t actually a constitutional
right, the scope of which is governed only by policy and
cost-benefit considerations. See Vega v. Tekoh , 597 U.S.
134, 136, 143-144, 152 (2022). Equally important, the
incorporation of such a non-right against the states via
the Due Process Clause is completely unsupported and
unsupportable.
It’s no answer that Miranda is chanted endlessly in
episodes of Law & Order, or that it may expand some
rights. See Amar Br. 15-17. Miranda and its progeny
“flagrantly offend[] fundamental principles of separation
of powers, and arrogate[] . . . prerogatives reserved to
the representatives of the people.” Dickerson v. United
States, 530 U.S. 428, 454 (2000) (Scalia, J., dissenting).
It violates the basic tenet of our republic that the people
have the power to regulate themselves—via Congress and
their State legislatures—in the absence of a constitutional
prohibition. Justice Scalia and Justice Thomas thus found
Miranda unworkable, “an illegitimate exercise of . . .
authority to review state court judgments,” and reflecting
“judicial arrogance,” such that it should be overruled. Id.
at 461, 465. In short, the argument for overruling Miranda
is far stronger than what Petitioner suggests justifies
overruling Williams.

14
2. Even confined to the realm of jury mechanics,
Petitioner invites widespread revanchment. For example,
on the same day this Court issued Williams, a plurality
held that the jury right attaches “where imprisonment
for more than six months is authorized.” Baldwin v. New
York, 399 U.S. 66, 69 (1970) (plurality op.). The plurality
identified no textual support, conceded that it was simply
“drawing a line,” and acknowledged that historical practice
included examples contrary to that line. 399 U.S. at 71, 73.
That’s the same weak sauce this Court found insufficient
in Ramos, 590 U.S. at 94 (recounting the “badly fractured
set of opinions” in Apodaca v. Oregon, 406 U.S. 404 (1972)).
And, once again, how can such an atextual and ahistorical
rule be incorporated against the states as a fundamental
right under the Due Process Clause?
3. The micromanagement of capital jury procedures
and the substantive availability of capital punishment
are particularly ripe for re-opening. See, e.g. , Gregg
v. Georgia , 428 U.S. 153 (1976). At common law, the
jury’s judgment of guilt in a capital case dictated the
punishment. Indeed, in Woodson v. North Carolina , 428
U.S. 280 (1976), the plurality acknowledged that as of 1791,
“the States uniformly followed the common-law practice
of making death the exclusive and mandatory sentence for
certain specified offenses,” including murder and rape. Id.
at 289. Lesser included offenses were the mechanism for
reduced sentences until the States adopted discretionary
capital sentencing. See id. at 291. Yet, suddenly, centuries
of practice were unconstitutional, even if they had been
softened by State legislatures. Justice Rehnquist cogently
pointed out the lack of originalist support for such judicial
micromanagement of State criminal law. Id. at 308-324
(Rehnquist, J., dissenting); see also, e.g. , An Act for the

15
Punishment of Crimes Against the United States, 1 Stat.
112 (1790) (persons guilty of treason, willful murder,
piracy, or robbery “shall suffer death”). Yet functionalism
prevailed. A plurality undertook a different, even more
pernicious form of micromanagement in Coker v. Georgia,
433 U.S. 584 (1977), holding that a violent, serial rapist
categorically could not be subject to capital punishment.
Then thirty years later, a bare majority bootstrapped
contortions-on-contortions to conclude the byzantine
“standards” this Court had imposed on capital punishment
in Gregg and its progeny were too “difficult” for a jury to
apply to a child rapist. Kennedy v. Louisiana , 554 U.S.
407, 439-441 (2008).
If “Apodaca [sat] uneasily with 120 years of preceding
caselaw,” Ramos , 590 U.S. at 106, cases like Gregg ,
Woodson, Coker, and Kennedy outright defy it, with the
upshot of denying the people’s right to legislate for their
own protection. The incorporation against the states of
these atextual and ahistorical “rights” bears more than
a whiff of substantive due process. 3
CONCLUSION
The Williams Court properly reviewed the historical
and textual evidence, acknowledged its lack of clarity, and
drew a clear rule by looking at the historical purpose of the
jury. That some might reach a different result if writing
on a clean slate is not grounds to overrule that precedent.
But if the Court does so, it should be even-more-receptive

Doctrine (2026), https://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7365499, at 23-33
and 47-51.

16
to overruling the criminal procedure precedents of the
1960s and 1970s.
